source.title: Quantum Information Theory: Results and Open Problems

accepted.question_text: What is a general formula for the capacity of an arbitrary quantum channel, that is, a formula that determines the ultimate asymptotic rate at which information can be transmitted reliably when the communication channel has genuinely quantum effects rather than being reducible to a classical channel or to a collection of special cases?

evidence.quote: This has not proven to be the case; even now, we do not have a general formula for the capacity of a quantum channel.

accepted.question_text: Suppose an ensemble consists of exactly two quantum states and one wants to maximize the accessible classical information obtained by measuring the received state. Must every measurement that attains this optimum be a von Neumann measurement, or can a more general positive-operator-valued measurement be strictly better even in the two-state case?

evidence.quote: If there are only two states in an ensemble, it has been conjectured that the measurement optimizing accessible information is always a von Neumann measurement, mainly because extensive computer experiments have not found a counterexample [11].
This conjecture has been proven for quantum states in two dimensions [22]. Our next example shows that this conjecture does not hold for ensembles composed of three or more states.

accepted.question_text: Let a memoryless quantum channel N have classical one-use quantity χ_max(N), defined as the maximum, over all ensembles of input states, of the Holevo quantity for the corresponding channel outputs. Is χ_max additive for all pairs of quantum channels, meaning χ_max(N1 ⊗ N2) = χ_max(N1) + χ_max(N2)? Equivalently, can entangling inputs across separate channel uses ever increase the achievable classical communication rate beyond what is obtained by optimizing one use at a time?
accepted.context_brief: Additivity of classical channel capacity quantity

evidence.quote: We do not know whether this is the capacity of a quantum channel; if the use of entanglement between separate inputs to the channel helps to increase channel capacity, it might be possible to exceed this χmax(N).
This can be addressed by answering a question that is simple to state: Is χmax(N) additive [1]?
That is, if we have two quantum channels N1 and N2, is χmax(N1 ⊗ N2)=χmax(N1)+χmax(N2).
The question is whether strictly more capacity can be attained by using the tensor product of two channels jointly than by using them separately.

accepted.question_text: For a mixed bipartite quantum state ρ, are the entanglement of formation and the distillable entanglement always equal? In other words, when two distant parties are restricted to local quantum operations and classical communication, does the asymptotic number of EPR pairs needed to create ρ always equal the asymptotic number of EPR pairs that can be extracted back from copies of ρ?

evidence.quote: If ρ is not a pure state, the situation becomes much more complicated.

In this case, we can define entanglement of formation (Ef), which is asympotitically the number of EPR pairs that we need to form ρ; and distillable entanglement (Ed), which is asymptotically the number of EPR pairs which can be created from ρ.
If ρ is pure, then these two quantities are equal, but this does not appear to be true if ρ is mixed.

accepted.question_text: For a mixed bipartite state ρ, does the entanglement of formation equal the one-shot entanglement of formation obtained by minimizing the average entanglement over pure-state ensembles whose density matrix is ρ? Equivalently, is the one-shot entanglement of formation additive, so that this single-letter expression really gives the asymptotic entanglement cost?
accepted.context_brief: Additivity of one-shot entanglement of formation

evidence.quote: Much like the classical capacity of a quantum channel, there is a nice expression which would be equal to the entanglement of formation if it could be proved to be additive.
We call it the one-shot entanglement of formation, and it is the minimum average entanglement over ensembles of pure states whose density matrix is ρ.

accepted.question_text: Let Q(N) denote the quantum capacity of a noisy quantum channel N, meaning the asymptotic rate at which quantum states can be transmitted reliably through N. Is Q(N) equal to the regularized coherent information expression obtained by maximizing the coherent information over n uses of the channel and then dividing by n in the limit n → ∞?

evidence.quote: There is a conjectured capacity formula for Q.
The quantity (36) is an upper bound for the quantum capacity of a noisy quantum channel N [2], and is conjectured to be equal to this capacity [19].
